title: Ashley Keating and Allan Whitworth Interview, 1963-03-22

pages.label: 001_Ashley Keating and Allan Whitworth Interview, 1963-03-22 Part 1

blocks.x: I got your hand broken. Now the light's on.
Let's see.
Now we have to turn this to tape?
Yeah, turn it to tape.
Okay, we're interviewing today at our Tilton Library,
Seminar Room 2, Tulane University. What's today's date, Alan or Ashley?
22nd, I think.

22nd of March, 1963 it is, isn't it? Okay. Can you give your name, Ashley, your first? I'll get you to give yours. Yes, Ashley Keating. And yours? Alan Whitworth. Oh, good. Miss Snapp, put your name on that.
Alright, Elizabeth Snapp.
Jack?
Jack Hurley.

Louder, huh? Jack Hurley. Okay. And my name is Dick Allen. And we just happened to be in here working. We decided to interview two gentlemen from Australia. You're first, Ashley. Let's see, where were you born anyhow?
In Wandi, a small town in Queensland, Australia, Dick. And when? 1939, December the 1st. December the 1st.
And did you hear jazz when you were growing up? Did you have any musicians in your family or anything?

My father, at one stage, won the Queensland Band Cornet Solo Championship. He was a relatively good musician, I'd say. I, at some stage of the game, when very small, can remember listening to Dixieland and having it appeal to me, not really knowing quite what it was. It was a pseudo type, I'd say. And soon, via Muggsy Spanier and bands of that ilk, the Bobcats, found out that I could get the sound the whole way through a record, not just parts of it. And that started my interest in the New Orleans style.
You came back through the Chicago and the Dixieland, I hope, people, to the New Orleans.
Yes, yes, that's for sure.
And, uh, did you play any instrument before you took up the banjo?

No, it was the first instrument. A last desperate effort, I'd say. I don't think I could have mastered anything else. Not that I've mastered this, but it was the one that could get me onto the scene quicker than any other, I'd say.
Uh-huh. And, uh, when did you start the banjo?
Uh, it'll be two and a half years ago now.
Two and a half years ago? Uh-huh. And did you have any lessons to start with?
Uh, yes, I had ten lessons from a, a woman teacher at the Queensland College of Music. Hmm.
They teach banjo at the Queensland College of Music?
Yes, they do. It's a commercial type of, uh, uh, solely teaches popular music. She taught me where to find the notes and a few chord formations. From there I pressed on on her own.
Did she have a clue about what you were trying to do?

Uh, she half understood, I think. She, she knew I wanted to play chords and wasn't particularly interested in becoming a virtuoso. But, uh, I don't think she knew who Lawrence Mariro was. And who is Lawrence Mariro to you? Uh, well, he still is everything I want to be as far as a musician goes. Uh, I can't recall ever hearing a more thrilling, uh, sound on the banjo.
I think we could use a little more volume there maybe, huh? Well, uh, did you, uh, play for fun with any groups or did you...?

Well, we had a group of our own and, uh, the principle of this group has always been to play for fun. Uh, I think they're pressing on even without Alan and myself. And, uh, the reason being purely and simply to give themselves enjoyment. Not to really entertain the public. Just to preserve the New Orleans sound or to try to, and to give themselves a lot of fun.
Uh, I see.

Uh, does it have a name or anything...? Uh, yes. We called the band the Bay City New Orleans Jazz Band. Uh, the bay portion of it coming from the fact that, uh, Brisbane is on, uh, a bay called Moreton Bay. And, uh, the New Orleans, uh, being added to denote devotion to the cause.
Mm-hmm. And you think of it as a cause, huh?
Uh, in Australia, for sure. And from what I've seen here, I'd say it's a cause, yes.
Consider yourself a fanatic?
Yes. Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.

Ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha. What do you think about the musicians here? Do you consider themselves... Do you think they consider themselves fanatics or do you think they're constantly making compromises or...?
Uh, uh, uh... From what I've seen...
That's why we're on the set.

From what I've seen, I...I wouldn't really term too many of them dedicated. I'd say this is just an on-the-spot review. I may live to regret this, but I'd say the Negro ones, which are the only ones I've really heard since I've been here, seem to play this way because they know no other way. But if there's a big crowd, they appear to me to certainly make concessions towards them. Perhaps it's through years of scuffling and hard going that they think they have to. Personally, I don't think they do. I think they'd get the people in, whether they played Gettysburg March instead of Bill Bailey or not.
I see. Back to the Bay City New Orleans Jazz Band, does it have any kind of San Francisco inspiration?

No, we did know of the Bay City Band with Sanford-Neubauer Everett-Farien Company. We liked it, but for us, we'd always preferred the ensemble, Lewis Johnson style, really. The fact that our band was called the Bay City didn't necessarily mean that it played in the tuba-laden West Coast style.
Mm-hmm. I see.

Who's in the band? The personnel at the time that Alan and I left consisted of Mike Hawthorne trumpet, Alex Jolliffe trombone, Martin Mooney clarinet, myself banjo, Alan drums, Tony McArthur bass, and Rod Byrne piano. No. Uh, well,
did, uh, you say Lewis Johnson, did any other bands have any influence on the band as a group?

Well, in view of the fact that there were seven people in the band who were playing for fun and had to be kept happy to stay in it, uh, and several members of the band could be termed perhaps Dixielanders if you didn't watch them, uh, I'd say, uh, possibly, uh, on the odd occasion an Eddie Condon influence or perhaps a Muggsy Spanier may have been able to creep in, but usually, uh, and even perhaps a Turk Murphy on some occasions, but, uh, by and large we tried to stick to the, uh, New Orleans marching style bands, as I said before, Lewis and company, for our inspiration.
And the people who played in the marching band? Not the,

not, you didn't have a brass band? No, we didn't have a brass band, but, uh, that, uh, type of, uh, music, perhaps we play, I think we would have played more marches and spirituals than we would have, say, blues.
Mm-hmm. How does it go over with the public?

Uh, well, we had, uh, quite a deal of success considering the, uh, narrow-mindedness of our, uh, cause. Uh, we had a steady, we had a steady Sunday night listening crowd of about, uh, between 40 to 80 depending on the weather and the conditions, but, uh, we were slowly educating the people. Uh, there was another band in town of, of a Dixieland variety that manages to drag in a couple of hundred, uh, but the people that attend there are sensation seekers rather than jazz lovers. I think we were doing our job reasonably well.
You think you have a different audience?

For sure, I'm certain. A much different audience. Uh, ours were, uh, young people, but they certainly wanted something out of the music rather than a loud noise, I think. They must have, if they came to hear us because they weren't going to get a great deal of technical proficiency, that's for sure.
Well, what about, uh, tell me a little more about the audience. I don't know about, like, are they working class people? Uh,

yes, uh, I, I, of course in Australia the social, uh, set up seems to be different. None of them would have been called either college or, uh, school children. They're all, uh, young working people. Most of the lads are either tradesmen or worked in a bank. The girls usually shop assistants, I'd say.
Record store.

Record stores or, uh, uh, just ordinary run-of-the-mill stenographers or typists. Certain, uh, English people that lived in the town, younger chaps that had helped take part in the revival in England also supported our band rather than the, uh, the other Dixieland band that was operating in town. But, uh, that sums up the crowd pretty thoroughly. I'd say they were definitely a working class person.
What did the English people have in their background that they liked?

Uh, the ones that came to our club were Collier fans, really. Possessed a few American music records and, uh, generally appreciated a sincere effort to play, uh, with hot tone, a bit of vibrato and, and an ensemble style. They seemed to shy away from the solos all-round principle, which, of course, gave them a similar outlook to us. As a matter of fact, the band jazz that replaced me, uh, when I left, I'm led to believe, comes from either Northern Ireland or, or England. I'm not quite sure.
What's his name?
Uh, Doug, Graham. Dougie Graham, that's right. I think he's played with Rodney Foster's Jazzmen, uh, a Northern Ireland group, much of the Chris Barber ilk.
Mm-hmm.
Needless to say, he's far better than me.
What are the other Australian bands like in general?

At the current time, there seems to be a, a fair, uh, swing towards the, uh, pianoless rhythm section and the, uh, Lewis-style clarinet. Uh, of course, there's still plenty of the older Australian-style jazz band, which is based on the, the Lou Watters West Coast style. I think if there is an Australian jazz style, that is it, uh, as exemplified by Graham Bell, Frank Johnson, and other bands, which I can't think of at the moment. Southern Jazz Band. The Southern Jazz Band, that's right, Dave Dalwitz's band. Uh, that type of, uh, style is, actually, I'd say, the Australian style. Uh, but, of late, in all the capital cities on the East Coast, that's Melbourne, Sydney, and Brisbane, there has been at least one or two Lewis-style bands functioning with a pianoless rhythm section, as I said, and the Lewis-style clarinet and strong vibrato from the trumpeter. Uh, they seem to meet, or to me, anyway, there seems to be a little, uh, either jealousy or disapproval on the part of the older jazz enthusiast, that's to say, the man of about, uh, 40, 45. Uh, he regards the other style as being, uh, the heritage of the young musician, and, uh, to suddenly come up with, with this style that is different. Uh, they seem to, uh, view it with a certain disdain. Uh, I think that was made pretty clear with the relatively cool reception Collier got from this vintage of jazz fan when he came to our convention in 1962.
How did Ken Collier get that? Whose idea was that?

Uh, the committee, uh, that was elected at the 1961 convention was instructed, uh, by the outgoing committee to, uh, make a search, uh, worldwide, uh, and to bring, uh, as a featured guest, a jazz man of note from some foreign country, preferably America, but, uh, England, or, as long as he was, uh, a jazz man with an international reputation. Uh, I believe several, uh, American jazz men were approached. Kid Orie was, uh, not feeling well. Turk Murphy was too busy. Uh, Louis Armstrong, of course, had other work. Uh, Lizzie Miles was asked also, but couldn't make it. George Lewis, uh, didn't feel he could make the trip. Uh, and, until finally it was narrowed down to white musicians, uh, such as Jimmy McPartland and Max Kaminsky, uh, both of who, uh, did reply, uh, both of whom, I suppose I should say, did reply, but, uh, made demands that the committee couldn't really meet. Uh, at a later date, McPartland came up with more suitable terms, but, uh, Collier had already been approached, uh, and had, uh, accepted to come. I believe the fee was a thousand pounds. That was to cover his first-class return airfare, uh, plus first-class accommodation, uh, and, uh, his entertainment for the five days he was there, or, it turned out to be longer. He was there about eight days, I think. Uh, I don't think there will be another guest artist, uh, asked, really. Uh, the committee that has just gone out, uh, instructed the incoming committee that, uh, if possible, it was to be avoided. Uh, apparently, public opinion was, or opinion amongst the jazz fan, that it was, uh, too expensive, and sooner or later, uh, the committee was going to run out of money at this rate. Seems a bit of a shame, really. I think they could have got a, perhaps a Negroid jazz man this time.
What is, uh, kind of, uh, committee is this? Explain it exactly. I don't get that.

Well, uh, as the things, uh, an annual, uh, convention, the jazz convention is an annual convention. Of course, it's like, uh, any other committee. They have a president, a secretary, a treasurer, uh, vice presidents, et cetera, uh, and it's placed in the hands of these men to see that, uh, a program is organized, halls are booked, uh, musicians in all states of Australia advised of, of the date and the, uh, locality of, of the convention, uh, and also to take care of such arrangements as, uh, billeting musicians and, uh, arranging social functions such as the picnic, the rorty old do, the jazz and a jug, um, and other,
uh,

functions which are traditional parts now of the, uh, conventions. There's been 17 of them and they occur every year from the 26th of December of that, of the year to the New Year's Day of the incoming year.
What is this, uh, functions that you're talking about? I can get the names of them.

Uh, uh, well, the rorty old do, uh, is, uh, an Australian term for a, a wild time, I'd say, and be the best way to put it. Uh, there's free beer, free food, uh, plenty of music, and, uh, a good time is had by all. Uh, uh, it's a traditional part of the, uh, conventions, there's been one every year, uh, the idea being to listen to the music while you're sober and, uh, then to make a complete mess of yourself once you become incoherent.
Ha, ha,
ha, ha, ha, And Australians alike then,
uh,
Yes, I'd say, even the non-jazz Australian, non-jazz loving Australian is a pretty hard doer as regards alcoholic beverages. Do you think transportation would help? Uh,
I,
I refrain from answering. Ha, ha, ha,
ha, ha, ha,
You wouldn't send them all to New Zealand? Uh, I don't think so. No. Well, how do you spell that rorty old do? Uh, R-O- T-Y. R-O- R-T-Y.
R-O-R-T-Y.

R-O-R-T-Y. I think so. It's, it's, it's, it's actually, it's an idiomatic term. I think it is R-O-R-T-Y-O-L-E-D-O. Uh, It's all one word? No, it's, it's three words. Three words. It's the rorty old do.
Then you said something about jazz and a jug.

Jazz and a jug, that's another excuse for getting drunk. Uh, that usually takes part at a, uh, an outer suburban hotel, uh, where the musicians are either transboarded by, uh, a riverboat. There's always a riverboat trip. And usually, uh, the riverboat trip, uh, terminates at some particular hotel where, uh, music is again played in the beer garden. And, uh, those who wish to destroy quite an amount of liquor can do so and listen to the music. And, uh, other traditional functions, uh, uh, usually on the first night of the convention also there's the how you've been keeping night where everyone, uh, makes, uh, renews their acquaintances from the previous year's convention. It's also another free, uh, grog night. Uh-huh.
I see.
Well,
uh, while we're talking about conventions and jazz clubs and these things, uh, are your jazz clubs over there for people who like jazz? Are they social organizations or both or what?

No, uh, with the exception of the Sydney Jazz Club, which is run by people who like jazz, uh, there's no denying that they have two bands playing there, uh, each Saturday night. Uh, with the exception of the Sydney Jazz Club, I'd say by and large the Australian Jazz Club, uh, is, is purely a social, social organization. Our club wasn't, but it's, it's so small that I, I'd hardly consider it a, uh, a force in Australian jazz. Any, any, uh, place where a jazz band plays, uh, in the other cities and, and could be called a jazz club, I would say with the exception of the Sydney Jazz Club, it, it's purely a social, uh, outlet. It's, uh, run more on the lines of a casual dance than a jazz club.
Now what's a jazz club? Is it like an English jazz club or an American jazz club?
Uh, I, I'd term it like an English jazz club. And, and people, who sponsors it in other words? Usually I think they're run by the band. Usually by the band. Um,
and people come there for what purpose?

Uh, some people would come to listen to the music, but, uh, most of them come to dance, uh, to talk to their friends, uh, especially while the music's playing, they seem to try and talk. Uh, by and large, they don't come to listen to the music. It's somewhere to go on Saturday or Sunday night. A lot of Australian jazz clubs are run on Sunday night. Now Sunday night in Australia is not like, uh, in the United States. Uh, everything closes Sunday. Uh, hotels, picture shows, everything. So there's nothing on, on Sunday night. If you want to take the girlfriend somewhere Sunday night, or you want somewhere to go yourself, you want somewhere where you can slip a bit of rum into your coke, well, you have to go to a jazz club. And consequently, they get a fringe audience. I don't think it's representative of the jazz listening public, really. Mm-hmm. I see.

Are Australians kind of prudes underneath it all, in addition to being heavy drinkers? Uh, I mean, in this, they have a blue law, what we call a blue law in this country, of closing everything down on Sunday, but worse than here.

Yes, well, uh, it is, it's much worse. Uh, in Brisbane, where we came from, uh, even Sunday sport, uh, while it went on, uh, there was a law to say that it was illegal, uh, of course the law is outdated, and the council are making moves to change that law, but, uh, even, it even made a game of golf on Sunday, in fact, illegal. So, and the same thing applies to entertainment, only more so. So, it would appear, as they, uh, your opinion there is correct.

Oh, how do you, uh, manage to play jazz? I mean, you have relatively small audiences, uh, you're running a jazz club. Does it make enough money to make it worth your while? You say primarily it's for fun.

Uh, we used to get about ten shillings a night, which amounts to a dollar each. Mm-hmm. Uh, we had a very small charge to get in. Usually people we knew very well we let in. The coffee lounge where we played, uh, we were given free. We had no rent. Uh, the only, uh, condition being that, uh, of course he could sell his, uh, drinks and sandwiches to the people who came in. It seemed to be worth his while, but if we were in it for the money, it most certainly wasn't worthwhile for us. It was for fun only.
How do you get by? How do you make it financial?
Well, uh, I should imagine a great deal of promotion to have to go into it. It's a thought that it, it never occurred to me.
No, I mean, you, you have to live. Well,
you have to eat every day. Yes, we have jobs during the day, unfortunately.
What do you do?
Uh, I was a motor mechanic by trade, but the last year I was in Australia, I worked as a spare parts, uh, salesman over the counter in a shop.
Mm-hmm.
It was a five day a week job, uh, not particularly hard, which allowed us to practice one night a week, and, uh, have the jazz club on the Sunday night.
Mm-hmm.
I see.

Uh, uh, I want to get a little more of the picture of things over there. In general, we have jazz clubs in this country, maybe you call them jazz organizations, or federations, or something over there. Uh, or do you have anything like that?

Uh, well, in each capital city, uh, well, no, in two of the capital cities, that's Sydney and, uh, Melbourne, uh, as I mentioned the Sydney Jazz Club before, that, that is an organization, which does present concerts on the odd occasion in the, in the, um, local town hall. And, similarly, Melbourne have, uh, flourishing jazz club, uh, but it seems to, uh, rely for support mainly upon the casual dancing public. But, uh, I, I suppose they would be termed parallel organizations to the New Orleans Jazz Club in this particular town. Uh,
they put out magazines,

they have radio programs? Yes, they, they put out magazines. Uh, neither of them have radio programs to my knowledge. Uh, uh, I think a radio program in Australia probably costs a fair deal more to sponsor than it does here. Uh, and for that, uh, coupled with the fact that it would not have a very large, uh, listening public, uh, they, they don't bother in that regard. But they do put out magazines. Uh, the Sydney Jazz Club put out quite a good magazine. It's called The Quarterly Rag. Uh, usually features photographs and some quite interesting articles.
Um, tell me about New Orleans when you got here. What did you think?

Uh, well, the first thing we noticed that we recognized, of course, was Canal Street. Uh, it was a big thrill to stand on Canal Street. I think we were on the widest street in the world. Uh, we were staying at the YMCA, as we walked up St Charles, and we came across names such as Perdido, uh, that meant, uh, quite a lot to us, far more than it would to the average tourist. I'd say they'd go completely unnoticed. Uh, we immediately thought in terms of the New Orleans Wanderers, King Oliver, that, uh, it's, uh, well, the culmination of, uh, something we've been dreaming about for a long while, to finally be here, to be rubbing shoulders with the musicians, and seeing all the names of the streets and places that we've, uh, so long for us anyway, have been either names in cultist books, or, uh, names on, on records that we treasure. It's great.
Tell me about, uh, the bands you've heard. You have heard some bands, you know.

Uh, uh, yes, we've heard quite a few. I'd say we've heard about ten, in, not as many days. Uh, well, the most inspired, band we've heard, has been a quartet. Uh, George Lewis, Jim Robinson, Joe Watkins, and, uh, Dolly Adams. It was last, Friday night, I think, at Preservation Hall. Anyway, it certainly reached a, a peak of emotion that left me shattered. The other band that impressed us most was, was Lewis, with, uh, Kid Howard, uh, Albert Warner, and, uh, a rhythm section, who I just forget now, I think, Cy Frazier, and, uh, Papa John. Papa John Joseph, that's right, he was the bass player. Uh, that, that was the, uh, those two would be the, the greatest moments we've had, in our listening career, I'm sure.
Where was this, you heard this last band?

At Preservation Hall. Mm-hmm. Uh, we've heard some, interesting things on the side as well. had interesting conversations with, uh, fellow jazz enthusiasts too. I think last night, was very enjoyable too. We were both impressed with the, uh, the Gibson Brass band. It was, great fun listening to them. And, particularly the conditions under which they were practicing. It reminded us a bit of the way we used to, press on regardless at home. All, keeped up in a small room, going around to one another's places to play. I think that's where the, the strength of the music lies, and it's, uh, folk appeal, really.
Well, what about the band? What impressed you about it?

Uh, well, strangely, the, the, one thing that did, uh, impress, well, not actually impressed me, but struck me, was the, the fact that they all seemed very broad-minded musically. They spoke in terms of Lawrence Welk, um, various Dixieland bands, and the tunes they played, weren't perhaps, uh, Panama, uh, other New Orleans, uh, type tunes, or the ones that we in Australia think are typical New Orleans tunes, but rather, uh, a better quality of pop song. Uh, but even though they did speak in terms of Lawrence Welk, and, and, uh, legitimate music, they all managed to play with, uh, hot tone and vibrato, which, uh, sure makes the thinkers that it's something that's born into them. It, it, it's nothing they have to try to do. It was, uh, seeing them at, at, at first hand, I'd say, and, uh, realizing that while there's lots of other musical influences exerted on them, the one that still predominates is, is the Negroid one.
I wonder about, uh, the different people in the band. What did you think of them as individuals? If you don't mind answering them.

No, I don't mind. Uh, well, as regards, uh, this is the Gibson band you're talking about. Yeah, the Gibson band. Yes. Uh, I was, I was impressed with, uh, Eddie Richardson to start with. Uh, he's the leader. I think he behaves as though he is. Yeah, he's the musical director. He's the, yes, that, uh, I, I would say he would be, by far the best musician. Uh, the trombonist, Carol Blunt, uh, also impressed. I don't know how he'd be in a jazz band, but he certainly did know how to drive it down in a, in a marching band. Uh, the Althaus seemed to, uh, to add a little tonal coloring with, uh, various out of tune phrases. Uh, but it still seemed to add to the charm of the music somehow. Uh, uh, Dave Bailey too. He was a bit. Uh, on his bass drum and cymbal. Uh, I think they were the outstanding members of the band. Uh, the second trumpeter who arrived later, I've forgotten his name. Well, first it was Sonny Williams, who, that's right. The older man, and rather soft, and that's funny. Yes,
that's right, yes.

And then, then the other one arrived later was John Wimbley. That's right. Yes, well, uh, he seemed to have, uh, a particularly good idea of playing second trumpet to me. Mm-hmm. Although from what I've, uh, read on Barry Martin records, et cetera, uh, Eddie Richardson is, uh, allegedly an ideal second trumpet. Uh, but Eddie Richardson to me seemed to be very powerful, and, in, in particularly good lip.

When he was with the Eureka, he's the guy who carried the melody with him, you know. Yeah. Not, not second trumpet. No, he, and with this he's, man, he's more featured. That's right. Yeah, so it would appear that way. Yeah, well, they have, uh, a funny kind of setup in the New Orleans brass band trumpet. There's no point in going into that now. Uh, let's see. What did you think of the, uh, alto player who arrived later, Earl Batiste?

Uh, he seemed a very good musician. Uh, being a dyed in the wool, uh, Bunk Johnson and Lewis fan, uh, to be quite frank, no saxophone, uh, really moves me. Although, uh, having heard Manuel Paul, uh, play tenor, I found that quite interesting. Uh, but this, uh, lad was obviously a good musician. There's no two ways about that. Again, he played with a fairly strong vibrato. Uh, I would have liked to have heard him on some other instrument. I think you suggested to him, he might perhaps like to play a soprano or a clarinet. Uh, I'd agree with you there. I think he, uh, probably would be much, uh,

easier to listen to on one of those instruments. Well, they said he'd been with various bands like Bull Moose Jackson and Ray Charles, and I hadn't expected anything which was generally in the New Orleans idiom that much out of somebody who'd been with those people. No, No, he seemed, he seemed to be familiar with what they were doing. He was conversing with,
there's nothing sure of. Yeah, and, and, uh, it's strange how those people pop out of, out of nowhere. He would have been relatively young too, I'd say, wouldn't he, about 25 or so?
Something like that.
No more.
The tuba player they seemed to like, and he's, what, something like 16 or 17.
That's right,

very young. They never did give me his name. He didn't play. He, he was there. That's, that's strange the way it, it goes. Uh, what about the bands at Preservation Hall and Dixieland Hall and the Paddock or anything like that? Have you heard those?

Uh, we've heard a couple at, uh, Dixieland Hall. Uh, unfortunately there seemed to be some pressure on them to play, uh, a tourist type of music. We didn't stay along in either case. Uh, one band was Paul Barberans, I think, and another one was led by Frog Jazz. Although the personnel of both bands seemed to be relatively similar. Uh, I don't think it had appealed.

pages.label: 002_Ashley Keating and Allan Whitworth Interview, 1963-03-22 Part 2

blocks.x: All right. See, this is a reel two of Ashley Keating and Alan Whitworth. All right, we were talking about your impression of Dixieland Hall and Hall Barber and Kit Howard's band there.

That's right, yes. Well, those bands seem to be under pressure to play a crowd-pleasing commercial style, certainly not of a great deal of interest to the enthusiast of New Orleans music. The paddock, we never did get inside. Of course, we're doing this on a limited budget and 90 cents for a drink is a little more than we can afford, particularly as we don't drink unless it's to hear some famous musician.

segments.title: Tape set-up, date and introductions
segments.summary: Allen sets up the recording at Tulane's Tilton Library, gives the date (22 March 1963) and has the participants state their names.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
segments.title: Growing up in Queensland, discovering New Orleans style, learning banjo
segments.summary: Keating was born in Queensland in 1939; his father was a cornet champion. Records by Muggsy Spanier led him to New Orleans style. He took up banjo about two and a half years earlier and had ten lessons.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
segments.title: The Bay City New Orleans Jazz Band: playing for fun
segments.summary: Keating describes his Brisbane amateur group, how it got its name, and why he thinks of the music as a cause.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
segments.title: Opinion of New Orleans musicians' dedication
segments.summary: Asked about the local musicians, Keating gives a first impression that they play the music naturally but make concessions to big crowds.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
segments.title: Bay City band's personnel, influences and repertoire
segments.summary: Keating lists the seven members, explains the name has no San Francisco link, and says they followed George Lewis's marching style with some Condon, Spanier and Turk Murphy influence, playing marches and spirituals.

segments.chapter: Early life and the Brisbane band
segments.title: The band's audience in Brisbane
segments.summary: The Sunday-night crowd of 40-80 young working people differed from the Dixieland band's audience; English fans of the revival supported them, and Doug Graham replaced Keating.

segments.title: Australian band styles and Ken Colyer's 1962 convention visit
segments.summary: Keating contrasts the older Australian West Coast style with newer Lewis-style bands, and explains how the convention committee chose Colyer after approaching several Americans.

segments.title: Australian jazz conventions and their traditional social events
segments.summary: Keating explains the committee that runs the annual convention and describes the rorty old do, jazz and a jug, and the how-you've-been-keeping night, with talk of drinking.

segments.title: Australian jazz clubs and Sunday blue laws
segments.summary: Keating says most Australian jazz clubs are social outlets where people dance and talk. Sunday closing laws make clubs the only place to go.

segments.title: Money and day jobs for a hobby band
segments.summary: The band earned about ten shillings a night each and played for fun; Keating worked as a motor mechanic and then a parts salesman.

segments.title: Jazz societies and magazines in Sydney and Melbourne
segments.summary: Sydney and Melbourne have jazz clubs that put out magazines such as The Quarterly Rag but no radio programs.

segments.title: First impressions of New Orleans
segments.summary: Keating recalls the thrill of seeing Canal Street and Perdido Street names familiar from records.

segments.title: Bands heard: George Lewis at Preservation Hall
segments.summary: The most inspiring sets were George Lewis's quartet and his band with Kid Howard at Preservation Hall.

segments.title: The Gibson Brass Band rehearsal and its musical outlook
segments.summary: Keating enjoyed the Gibson Brass Band's rehearsal, noting its folk feel and the members' broad musical tastes alongside a hot tone and vibrato.

segments.title: Individual members of the Gibson band
segments.summary: Keating gives opinions on Eddie Richardson, the trombonist, Dave Bailey and the trumpeters Sonny Williams and John Wimbley.

segments.title: The alto player and the young tuba player
segments.summary: Keating and Allen discuss alto saxophonist Earl Batiste, who had played with R&B bands, Keating's dislike of saxophone, and the very young tuba player.

segments.title: Dixieland Hall, the Paddock and tourist-oriented music
segments.summary: Keating says the bands at Dixieland Hall played crowd-pleasing commercial music, and he could not afford the Paddock.
